questions.question: Which causes of drug shortage does the revised TR-68 mainly address, and up to which point in the supply chain does its scope extend?

options.A: Shortages from all causes, with the scope running from raw materials all the way to the final distribution end at pharmacies and hospitals and to the patient
options.B: Shortages caused by manufacturing and quality problems, with the scope ending at batch release and handover to the first economic customer
options.C: Shortages caused by commercial and economic factors, with the scope ending when the wholesaler delivers the drug to the hospital
options.D: Shortages caused by sterile drug product manufacturing, with the scope including wholesale and retail channels after batch release

questions.explanation: TR-68 focuses on shortages caused by manufacturing and quality problems, up to batch release; after handover to the first economic customer the MAH usually has no visibility, so this is out of scope. However, if the MAH is also responsible for distribution, TR-68 still applies.

questions.question: TR-68 cites the definition of harm in ICH Q9(R1). Which of the following is correct?

options.A: Damage to health caused by poor drug quality or adverse reactions; supply interruption is a commercial issue rather than harm and is outside the scope of QRM
options.B: Patient death or irreversible injury; minor inconvenience or treatment delay is not within the scope of harm
options.C: Damage to health caused by adverse drug reactions; supply and accessibility problems are not within the definition
options.D: Damage to health, including damage that can occur from loss of product quality or availability

questions.explanation: ICH Q9(R1) includes unavailability (availability) in harm, which is exactly the basis on which TR-68 treats drug shortage as a QRM issue. Statements that mention only quality or adverse reactions leave out availability.

questions.question: After a company has implemented controls such as dual sourcing and higher safety stock, the shortage risk that remains is called what in the glossary?

options.A: Residual Risk
options.B: Risk Priority Level
options.C: Critical Shortage (a shortage with no alternative therapy)
options.D: Potential Drug Shortage

questions.explanation: Residual Risk is the risk remaining after risk control measures have been implemented; in a shortage context, it is the shortage risk that still exists after controls. Risk Priority Level is a relative level used to prioritize handling; it is not the risk remaining after control.

questions.question: According to the glossary, which of the following best matches the definition of Meaningful Disruption?

options.A: Any production interruption, including routine maintenance and minor process changes expected to be restored soon
options.B: A situation that exists only when the drug is already out of stock nationwide, patients actually cannot obtain it, and healthcare institutions have reported it
options.C: A change in production that is reasonably likely to lead to a reduction in supply of a drug that is more than negligible and affects the ability to meet expected demand
options.D: An event that must be formally declared a shortage by the health authority, with production stoppage expected to exceed one year

questions.explanation: The key to Meaningful Disruption is a change that is reasonably likely to reduce supply by more than a negligible amount and affects the ability to ship or to meet expected demand. Routine maintenance and minor changes expected to be restored shortly do not count.

questions.question: A drug is temporarily out of stock in one county or city because of a distribution delay, but the national supply as a whole is sufficient to meet demand. How should this be viewed under the glossary definition of shortage?

options.A: A shortage in any region constitutes a drug shortage and must be reported immediately
options.B: It is a short-term, localized logistical issue and should not be counted as a drug shortage
options.C: It is a Critical Shortage, because patients in that region temporarily have no alternative therapy available
options.D: It should be treated as a Potential Drug Shortage, and an immediate reassessment of the overall risk should be required

questions.explanation: The glossary defines shortage as an imbalance of supply and demand at the national level; regional supply interruptions caused by distribution difficulties, redistribution within the country, and the like are short-term, localized logistical issues and are not considered. A Critical Shortage refers to a shortage for which there is no alternative therapy.

questions.question: TR-68 uses "The Great Acetonitrile Shortage" as an example. Which events caused this global shortage?

options.A: Two major Chinese manufacturers went out of business because of the 2008 financial crisis, and new European regulations banned the use of the solvent
options.B: A Texas refinery was permanently closed by a 2008 hurricane, and China imposed an export ban on the solvent
options.C: Two major Chinese manufacturers stopped production to reduce air pollution for the 2008 Summer Olympics, and a Texas hurricane disrupted production
options.D: Major manufacturers worldwide were shut down for GMP non-compliance, and the COVID-19 pandemic caused a surge in demand

questions.explanation: The two major manufacturers were located in the same area of China and were required to stop production to reduce air pollution for the Olympics; a few months later, a Gulf of Mexico hurricane disrupted production in Texas, and the combination caused shortages of many APIs and drug products. The example shows that shortages can be very sudden and hard to predict.

questions.question: According to TR-68, what is the FDA definition of drug shortage?

options.A: A period of time when the demand or projected demand for the drug within the United States exceeds the supply of the drug
options.B: A national-level supply that is insufficient to meet demand, excluding short-term, localized logistical issues
options.C: A supply of a drug that the health system has determined to be essential that is insufficient to meet public health needs
options.D: A situation in which a disruption in the manufacturing supply chain prevents continuous supply of the drug to patients

questions.explanation: The FDA definition is a period of time when the demand or projected demand within the United States exceeds the supply. The wording "national level, excluding short-term logistical issues" reflects the direction of the 2019 EMA update, and "insufficient supply of a drug the health system determines to be essential" is the WHO wording.

questions.question: In August 2014, guidance was added as 5.71 in EudraLex Vol. 4 Part 1 Chapter 5. What is its main content?

options.A: Manufacturers must submit an annual shortage report to parliament explaining the cause of shortage for each product
options.B: Manufacturers must publish stock levels and expected resupply dates for each product directly to the public
options.C: Wholesalers must prioritize delivery to hospitals during a shortage and report each channel's delivery records and stock to the MAH item by item
options.D: Any restriction in supply should be notified to the MAH in a timely manner so that the MAH can report to the relevant competent authorities

questions.explanation: Section 5.71 requires that notification of restrictions in supply be timely so that the MAH can report to the relevant competent authorities. Annual reporting to Congress is a requirement of the amended US Section 506C and is unrelated to EU 5.71.

questions.topic: When a shortage starts in the value chain
questions.question: According to the TR-68 section 3.3 view of the value chain, at what point has a drug shortage already begun?

options.A: When a finished product batch fails QC testing, is rejected, and cannot be released to market, interrupting subsequent supply
options.B: When API, excipients, starting materials, reagents, solvents, components, or packaging materials cannot be supplied to the manufacturing process
options.C: When a pharmacy or hospital reports an out-of-stock and the health authority officially announces a shortage of the drug
options.D: When the wholesaler's stock falls below safety stock and it can no longer place new orders with the MAH

questions.explanation: Section 3.3 states that a shortage has already started in the value chain as soon as any material or component cannot be supplied to the manufacturing process, without waiting for the finished product to be out of stock. This is why an end-to-end value chain risk assessment is needed.

questions.question: An MAH outsources the production of a sterile injectable to a CDMO, and the CDMO's capacity constraints may affect supply. According to TR-68 management accountability, how should this be handled?

options.A: The MAH remains responsible for overseeing and mitigating the CDMO's quality and supply risks, and sets quality and capacity expectations in the contract
options.B: Responsibility has transferred to the CDMO; the MAH only needs to notify the health authority after a shortage occurs, and quality events are the CDMO's own responsibility
options.C: The wholesaler is responsible, because wholesalers have a general service obligation to get drugs to patients
options.D: The health authority is responsible for coordination, and the MAH does not need to agree on capacity matters with the CDMO in advance

questions.explanation: The MAH's senior management is ultimately responsible for ensuring supply, including oversight and risk mitigation of third parties such as CDMOs and contract laboratories, and the contract should clearly set expectations for quality and capacity constraints. A wholesaler's obligation is to get drugs to patients; it is not the MAH's manufacturing risk.

questions.question: TR-68 section 5.0 divides the elements of shortage prevention into product level and system level. What is the focus of each?

options.A: Product level is a robust PQS and appropriate oversight; system level is understanding the end-to-end value chain to implement controls and inventory allocation
options.B: Product level is the timing of communication with health authorities; system level is the principles for allocating inventory across markets
options.C: Product level is setting investment priorities by budget; system level is setting the strength of controls by product selling price
options.D: Product level is understanding the end-to-end value chain to implement end-to-end controls; system level is appropriate oversight and a robust PQS

questions.explanation: The product level relies on an understanding of the end-to-end value chain to put controls in place, and the system level relies on appropriate oversight and a robust PQS to ensure regulatory compliance. The first option swaps the two, which is a common confusion.

questions.topic: QRM and KM as PQS enablers
questions.question: According to ICH Q10 as cited in section 5.1, what role do QRM and knowledge management play in the PQS?

options.A: They are outputs of the PQS, compiled only at the annual management review and submitted by senior management to the regulator for record
options.B: They can replace the CAPA system, so a company no longer needs to maintain corrective and preventive actions separately
options.C: They are enablers of the PQS that help the practical integration of the PQS elements to improve drug quality and availability
options.D: They are specific to the development stage, and are not needed for process and product monitoring after commercial manufacturing

questions.explanation: ICH Q10 treats QRM and knowledge management as enablers of the PQS, used to integrate the PQS elements. ICH Q10 also requires continued monitoring of processes and products during commercial manufacturing, and this information is exactly the source of knowledge management.

questions.question: TR-68 section 5.1 states that the education and qualification training of personnel who handle deviations should include, in addition to the deviation itself, which of the following?

options.A: Calculating batch yield loss and converting it into financial loss as the basis for the annual budget
options.B: Assessing the potential impact on supply if the problem were to escalate further
options.C: Assessing competitors' pricing strategies to decide whether market prices need adjusting
options.D: Deciding whether to make a direct statement to the media to avoid outside speculation about the shortage

questions.explanation: Personnel who handle GMP and regulatory compliance deviations must be able to quickly identify potential problems and assess the impact on supply, and an escalation mechanism should be established so that problems needing resources or alternatives reach the appropriate level of management. This is so that deviations are dealt with before they evolve into a shortage.

questions.question: According to section 5.2, when should the MAH interact early with the relevant health authority?

options.A: When a meaningful disruption in supply is anticipated
options.B: Only after the shortage has already harmed patients and has been reported in the media
options.C: Only when the company's product has been classified as Risk Level C and confirmed to have no impact on patients
options.D: Only when the health authority writes on its own initiative to ask about the current stock status

questions.explanation: Both the EU and the US have legal requirements to report potential shortages, so early interaction with the HA should begin when a meaningful disruption is anticipated. Acting only after patients are affected or the HA asks means the opportunity for prevention has been missed.

questions.question: Why does section 5.2 say that risk assessment helps with interaction with health authorities?

options.A: Health authorities only deal with Risk Level C shortages, and risk assessment helps a company downgrade
options.B: The result of a risk assessment can replace notification to the health authority, thereby exempting the company from the legal reporting obligation
options.C: Health authorities do not have the resources to intervene in all shortages, and risk assessment helps identify which shortages need their attention
options.D: Risk assessment lets a company decide on its own whether a shortage affects patients, with no need for further dialogue with the health authority

questions.explanation: Health authorities generally take a risk-based approach and do not have the resources to examine every shortage in depth; robust risk assessment and knowledge management help determine which shortages affect patients and need their involvement. Risk assessment cannot replace statutory reporting.

questions.question: A product is used for an acute short-term or chronic long-term disease; without treatment it would cause serious but reversible harm, and alternatives with a similar therapy are available on the market. Under the three-step risk classification, what is the Step 1 impact level?

options.A: Risk Level B (yellow)
options.B: Risk Level A (red)
options.C: Risk Level C (green)
options.D: Risk Priority Level 2

questions.explanation: For an acute short-term or chronic long-term disease with alternatives of a similar therapy available, Table 6.1.1-1 gives Risk Level B. Level A applies only when there is no alternative, and Level C applies when the same product has other dosage forms available. Priority Level is the output of Step 3, not of Step 1.

questions.question: A product has Risk Level C in Step 1, but the likelihood of shortage assessed in Step 2 is high. According to Table 6.1.3-1, what is the Step 3 Risk Priority Level?

options.A: Risk Priority Level 1
options.B: Risk Priority Level 2
options.C: Risk Priority Level 3
options.D: No priority level needs to be assigned

questions.explanation: Risk Level C combined with a high likelihood results in Priority Level 2; it is a medium or low likelihood that results in Level 3. A high likelihood raises the otherwise lowest impact level by one level.

questions.question: According to section 6.2, how should an effective value stream mapping team be composed and led?

options.A: Composed of the quality assurance department alone, to avoid influence from the opinions of shop-floor staff, with the QA head guiding and approving the conclusions
options.B: Composed of supply chain planners alone, focusing on inventory figures, guided by the department head
options.C: Composed of senior executives and external consultants, excluding front-line staff, to avoid losing focus in discussion
options.D: Cross-functional and familiar with manufacturing and supply processes, including laboratory technicians and operators, and facilitated by an objective, neutral person

questions.explanation: TR-68 notes that the most successful mapping exercises include laboratory technicians and operators and require good facilitation, preferably by an objective, neutral person. The team must be cross-functional and familiar with the processes and equipment in order to find the real stress points.

questions.question: According to section 6.3.3, how is periodic evaluation recommended for lifecycle management of the analytical control system (methods, specifications, and reference standards) of a commercial product?

options.A: Replace the analytical method once every year, to ensure the latest analytical technology on the market is always used
options.B: Reassess before every batch release, to ensure the specification is consistent with process capability
options.C: Review periodically, for example every five years, rather than only when an investigation finds a problem with the control system
options.D: Review only after an out-of-specification (OOS) investigation, to save resources

questions.explanation: Section 6.3.3 recommends reviewing periodically (for example, every five years) whether the analytical control system still controls quality, and not only when an investigation reveals a problem. Revising a control system can take two to five years, so planning ahead is all the more important.

questions.question: Facility B is approved in several countries to manufacture a product and meets Country 1's GMP expectations, but is not yet approved in Country 1. Demand in Country 1 suddenly rises and Facility A has insufficient capacity. According to section 6.4, what is the more appropriate approach?

options.A: Ship directly from Facility B to Country 1 first, and submit the PAC and explain to the health authority afterwards once supply has stabilized
options.B: Require Facility A to produce beyond its approved capacity and reduce Country 1's allocation
options.C: Wait for Country 1's normal review timeline, without communicating with the health authority in the meantime
options.D: Communicate with the Country 1 health authority and request an expedited review of the PAC application for Facility B

questions.explanation: The example in section 6.4 is exactly to ask Country 1 for an expedited review and approval of the PAC for Facility B, and to explain that patients will not be exposed to additional risk from the change. Shipping without approval, or waiting without communication, is not consistent with the document's approach.

questions.question: The first component of the Drug Shortage Prevention and Response Plan is "Identify Shortage Hazards". How far does its end-to-end risk assessment extend?

options.A: Up to the point of actual patient use, including dispensing at pharmacies and hospitals
options.B: The value chain up to the first economic customer, including manufacturing, storage, and transportation
options.C: Only inside the manufacturing site, from material receipt to finished product packaging and release
options.D: Up to batch release, excluding storage and transportation, because these are the distributor's responsibility

questions.explanation: The plan's E2E risk assessment extends to the first economic customer and includes manufacturing operations, storage, and transportation; the MAH's visibility generally ends once the product is shipped to the wholesaler.

questions.question: According to section 8.1, which of the following is core notification content to the health authority, rather than secondary supplementary information?

options.A: The Step 1 Risk Level and the expected duration
options.B: The names and addresses of the main distributors, and whether there are secondary wholesalers and their supply channels
options.C: The product's monthly prescription volume and current market share, for assessing the scale of impact
options.D: Whether government- or regulator-required stockpiling rules exist in each country or region, and the expected restocking date

questions.explanation: Core notification content includes MAH and product details, the cause of the shortage, the Step 1 Risk Level, the expected duration, the actions taken or planned, the affected countries, and the notification of other parties. Distribution, patient, and inventory information are secondary information that helps both sides build a shared understanding.

questions.question: Which of the following is a situation that should trigger a review and update of the Drug Shortage Prevention and Response Plan?

options.A: Routine preventive maintenance is completed as scheduled and the maintenance records are approved by QA
options.B: Employees complete their annual GMP training and all pass the test
options.C: The internal audit schedule is changed from once a year to twice a year
options.D: A manufacturing site is shut down or its GMP certificate is revoked

questions.explanation: The Plan is a living document and must be updated when the product's risk profile changes, for example a new indication or new market, approval of a new alternative, a facility shutdown or GMP certificate revocation, stock below target, rising usage, or new quality or manufacturing problems. Completion of routine maintenance and training does not change the risk profile.

questions.question: According to section 8.0, when must the relevant health authority be notified?

options.A: Only after patient harm has occurred, patient groups have formally complained to the health authority, and the media has reported widely
options.B: Only when the product is Risk Level A and its alternatives are also out of stock
options.C: When a meaningful disruption may occur because of manufacturing and quality problems, that is, when normal quantities of the drug cannot be delivered to distribution
options.D: Only when the health authority writes on its own initiative, or asks the company for inventory and sales data

questions.explanation: Section 8.0 states that when manufacturing and quality problems may cause a meaningful disruption, that is, when normal quantities cannot be delivered for further distribution, the health authorities in the regions where the product is marketed and a shortage is expected must be notified. Notification is not to be done only after patients are harmed or when asked.

questions.question: A health authority is considering whether to allow an MAH to import a version of the product originally supplied to another market (possibly with packaging in a different language). What kind of decision is this?

options.A: Whether to help obtain alternative supply sources
options.B: Whether to formally intervene in the management or coordination of the shortage
options.C: Whether to expedite approval of alternative sites or PACs
options.D: Whether to adopt a specific communication strategy in response to the shortage

questions.explanation: One of the health authority decisions listed in section 8.2 is helping to obtain alternative supply, including whether to allow import of another market's version, whether repackaging is needed, and whether to inform healthcare professionals that an unauthorized version is available. Expedited approval and communication strategy are two other, separate decisions.

questions.topic: Conclusions - rigor scales with patient risk
questions.question: According to the conclusions in section 9.0, how should an organization respond when the risk of a drug shortage to the patient population increases?

options.A: Maintain the same intensity of risk management and focus resources on reducing manufacturing costs and inventory holding costs
options.B: Narrow the scope of risk assessment, dealing only with cases confirmed to cause patient harm and with major deviations
options.C: Increase the rigor, effort, and cross-functional collaboration in addressing the risk, and communicate effectively with stakeholders
options.D: Reduce external communication to avoid market panic, until the shortage has caused an actual stock-out

questions.explanation: The conclusion stresses that the higher the risk to patients, the higher the organization's rigor, effort, and cross-functional collaboration should be, together with effective communication with health authorities and other stakeholders. Narrowing the scope or reducing communication is contrary to this principle.

questions.topic: Conclusions - PAC management plans and gCP
questions.question: Section 9.0 mentions how industry can work with health authorities to reduce shortage risk caused by, for example, aging facilities. How?

options.A: Have health authorities of each country waive review of all PACs, with companies declaring changes themselves and filing afterwards
options.B: Use mutually agreed PAC management plans and harmonized gCPs, requesting expedited review from multiple countries
options.C: Once approved by a single country, all other countries automatically recognize it, and the company need not file separately
options.D: The company reports all changes together after they are completed, without discussing them with health authorities beforehand

questions.explanation: The conclusion states that, through mutually agreed PAC management plans and harmonized gCPs, expedited review of certain PACs can be requested from multiple health authorities, helping companies to renew facilities and introduce new technologies. This does not mean exemption from review, nor automatic mutual recognition.

questions.question: In the Drug Shortage Risk Register template, how is the "Potential Drug Shortage Hazard" field recommended to describe the risk?

options.A: With a CAPA number in place of a description, to avoid text that is inconsistent with other documents
options.B: As a probability value calculated by statistical methods, with no text description
options.C: By citing GMP regulatory provisions one by one and explaining how each provision was violated
options.D: Briefly, in the style of a newspaper headline, citing relevant references where necessary

questions.explanation: The template says this field describes the risk in "newspaper headline style", with a reference added where necessary. The root cause or risk assessment title goes in a different column, "Hazardous Situations".

questions.question: In the Risk Register template, on what basis is the risk level in the "Initial Risk Level" field determined?

options.A: Considering the current shortage prevention controls and their likely effectiveness
options.B: Without considering any existing controls, based only on the inherent characteristics of the product
options.C: Based on annual revenue and profit contribution, estimating the financial loss from stopping supply
options.D: Based on supplier audit scores, to decide whether new controls need to be started

questions.explanation: The template explains that the Initial Risk Level is judged on the basis of current shortage prevention controls and their likely effectiveness, while the risk after implementation of control measures is recorded in Risk Level After Risk Control.

questions.question: For the Drug Shortage Prevention and Response Plan template in Appendix 2, on what unit basis is it recommended that one be completed for each?

options.A: Each manufacturing site or independent facility unit
options.B: Each marketed country or market region
options.C: Each API and its raw material sources
options.D: Each dosage form

questions.explanation: The beginning of the template explains that this triage model should be completed for each dosage form to assess product classification, impact on patients, and end-to-end controls, and it can be used for proactive prevention as well as for reactive response to a shortage.
